analysis.one_liner: Sweeping energy bill giving tax breaks, drilling access, and liability shields to energy industries alongside efficiency aid.
analysis.headline: Both chambers passed versions of the energy bill, but the final compromise died in the Senate when a vote to end debate got 57 of the 60 votes needed.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 6 was a thousand-page energy bill touching nearly everything: oil and gas drilling on federal lands, nuclear liability, electric utility regulation, ethanol mandates, appliance standards, and tax credits. It would have handed oil, gas, and nuclear companies tax breaks, royalty relief, and protection from some lawsuits, while also extending low-income heating aid and creating tax credits for energy-efficient homes and appliances. The House and Senate each passed a version, but the negotiated compromise fell three votes short in the Senate and never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers gain tax credits, royalty relief, expanded leasing on federal lands, and exclusion of hydraulic fracturing from Safe Drinking Water Act rules. Fuel additive makers gain a shield from lawsuits over fuel contamination. Nuclear companies keep the federal liability backstop behind their plants. Ethanol and renewable electricity producers gain guaranteed markets and extended tax credits. Homeowners gain credits for solar panels and efficiency upgrades, and low-income households gain extended heating assistance.

how_it_helps.text: Extends Low Income Home Energy Assistance and weatherization programs through fiscal 2006, and funds energy-efficiency grants for low-income communities.
Creates tax credits for residential solar equipment, energy-efficient new homes, efficiency improvements to existing homes, efficient appliances, and fuel-cell vehicles.
Requires utilities, on customer request, to provide net metering and real-time or time-of-use pricing, and directs the FTC to ban 'slamming' and 'cramming' of electric customers.
Creates enforceable federal reliability standards for the bulk-power electric grid, subject to Federal Energy Regulatory Commission review.
Extends the renewable electricity production tax credit to wind, biomass, geothermal, solar, and other sources.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of the industry tax credits and forgone royalty revenue. People whose drinking water is contaminated by the fuel additive MTBE would lose the ability to sue the makers of the additive. Communities near nuclear plants continue to bear accident risk above the federally indemnified cap, and land affected by expanded drilling and fracturing bears the environmental cost.

drawbacks.text: Establishes a 'safe harbor' shielding MTBE fuel from product liability claims, shifting the cost of water contamination away from fuel makers; it also authorizes funding for MTBE cleanup and transition grants for MTBE producers.
Amends the Safe Drinking Water Act to exclude hydraulic fracturing from the definition of underground injection, removing that activity from the underground injection control program.

The House version would have opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas leasing, shortened judicial review to 90 days, and limited the grounds for challenging lease sales.
Grants royalty relief and suspensions for deep gas in the Gulf of Mexico and offshore Alaska, and sets a mechanism letting lessees pay states 44 cents per dollar of federal royalty withheld.
Repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, lifting Depression-era restrictions on utility holding companies while substituting narrower FERC record-access rules.
Provides tax credits for marginal-well oil and gas production and suspends the taxable-income limit on percentage depletion for oil and gas producers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer side of the bill was real: heating aid for low-income households, efficiency tax credits, appliance standards, and enforceable grid reliability rules. But the bill's largest and most specific financial benefits flowed to concentrated interests: liability protection for MTBE makers, a drilling exemption for hydraulic fracturing, royalty givebacks, and targeted oil and gas tax breaks. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the same bill shifted contamination and accident costs from those industries onto the public.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the negotiated compromise 246-180, but the Senate never got an up-or-down vote on it: a motion to end debate and proceed to a final vote won only 57 of the 60 votes needed, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed the Energy Policy Act of 2003 on April 11, 2003, by a recorded vote of 247-175, with 207 of 229 Republicans in favor and only 40 of 205 Democrats.
The Senate passed its own amended version on July 31, 2003, by 84-14, with strong support from both parties.
The two versions went to a conference committee, and the conference report was filed on November 18, 2003.
The House adopted the conference report 246-180 on November 18, 2003, again with 200 of 229 Republicans for and 46 of 205 Democrats for.

In the Senate, cloture on the conference report — the vote needed to end debate and reach a final vote — failed on November 21, 2003, 57-40, short of the 60 required; 32 of 48 Democrats and 7 of 51 Republicans voted no.
With the Senate unable to reach a final vote, the bill never became law, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people with the most immediate win were those who would have lost lawsuit rights under the MTBE liability shield, which died with the bill. The industries that had negotiated the tax breaks and royalty relief got nothing from this version — though their backers retained both chambers' majorities and returned with a successor energy bill in the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: MTBE plaintiffs kept suing; industry backers regrouped

sides.party_line_note: Early votes were lopsided and bipartisan: the House passed its version 247-175 (207 R, 40 D) and the Senate passed its version 84-14 (48 R, 35 D), but the final compromise split harder — 32 of 48 Senate Democrats and 7 of 51 Senate Republicans voted against ending debate, with the fuel-additive liability shield the reported sticking point.

industries.note: The bill would give production tax credits, royalty relief and suspensions for deep gas in the Gulf and offshore Alaska, expanded federal leasing including the Arctic Refuge coastal plain in the House version, and exemption of hydraulic fracturing from Safe Drinking Water Act rules. The benefits are targeted industry write-offs while the liability and environmental costs land on the public.

The bill creates a safe harbor from product liability suits over MTBE, the gasoline additive that contaminated groundwater in many states, and funds cleanup plus producer transition grants. The shield transfers contamination costs from the companies to water users and communities.

The bill extends the Price-Anderson federal indemnification of nuclear licensees through 2017 and makes DOE contractor indemnity permanent, while funding nuclear research programs. This locks in the structure in which plant accident liability above a cap is backstopped by the federal government, i.e., taxpayers.

The bill repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, freeing utility holding companies from longstanding structural restrictions, while adding FERC and state access to books and records and new enforceable reliability standards. Reliability rules protect consumers after the 2003 grid failure, but the core deregulation serves the companies.

The bill mandates rising volumes of renewable fuel in gasoline and adds credits for small ethanol producers, guaranteeing a market for ethanol makers. Consumers share the cost of the mandate through fuel prices, while farm-state economies gain.

The bill extends and broadens the renewable electricity production tax credit to wind, biomass, geothermal, solar, and other sources, and funds renewable research and rural electrification grants. These provisions serve both producers and ratepayers seeking alternatives to fossil generation.
